Fourteen months after thymectomy, painful muscle spasms returned and were only moderately controlled by diazepam and baclofen. Again, a 5-day course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) was administered and this produced marked clinical improvement. Twenty-nine months after thymectomy, the patient again had a recurrence of symptoms. At that time, a 3-day course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) was administered, which produced marked clinical improvement.

Since no anti-GAD antibodies were seen in our case, and since abolition of muscular hyperactivity with general anesthesia can also be seen in voluntary muscular hyperactivity and tetanus, these diagnoses were briefly entertained. However, in this patient, continuous, involuntary MUP discharges in the gastrocnemius were documented at rest, which actually resembled myokymia clinically. It was these discharges that were abolished under general anesthesia (Fig. 1). This observation, accompanied by the patient’s predictable recurrence of symptoms (on average every 14 months) and favorable response to intravenous IgG on those occasions, suggested that the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than that of voluntary muscular overactivity. Similar to tetanus, the silent period in masseter muscle testing in this case was absent; however, the lack of history of a wound or trauma, the duration and persistence of symptoms after being treated with antitetanus immune globulin, and the lack of other common signs of tetanus such as trismus and risus sardonicus suggested that the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than that of ‘‘chronic’’ tetanus.

extractions.value: Approximately 2 months after thymectomy, the patient complained of diplopia. Examination showed weakness in the right lateral rectus and left medial rectus muscles. A Tensilon test at that time was negative. His eye movement abnormalities persisted and 2 weeks later he developed right facial weakness. Prostigmine injection of 1.5 mg given intramuscularly resulted in marked improvement of extraocular eye movements. He was temporarily maintained on pyridostigmine alone (60 mg q.i.d. and one Timespan 180 mg q.h.s.), but within 12 months was tapered off this and is presently asymptomatic for myasthenia gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies remain undetectable.
